title: Answer to Question: On the Reports Speaking of the End of the Financial Crisis and Signs of Economic Recovery
text:
Answer to Question: On the Reports Speaking of the End of the Financial Crisis and Signs of Economic Recovery

Question:

Western media recently published estimates by press companies to the effect that the worst stages of the financial crisis have ended, and that signs of economic recovery have begun to appear in some of the economies of the Western states, which is considered the first fruit of the efforts that were exerted. These press reports mentioned the opinions of economic and political experts who are optimistic about the stock exchanges and bank profits, and their saying that the return of the price of oil to rising is an indicator that the world economy has reached its lowest levels and begun to recover, which led to its prices rising again! So is there really a recovery in the economy? And if it is not so, but rather merely media bubbles to restore confidence in the world financial system, then what made these phenomena appear in shares and commodities on the stock exchanges, and in the rise of the price of petroleum?

Answer:

It is a mistake to look at financial indicators alone, such as looking at the rise in the value of the financial markets or the rise in commodity prices, to judge the recovery of the economy. Rather, it is necessary to look at the volume of companies' production, the total national income, the numbers of the unemployed, the prices of goods to the consumer, the volume of consumers' and companies' expenditure, the numbers of mortgaged homes, and the cases of declared bankruptcy, which have reached long-established companies such as General Motors..., and other economic phenomena. Then it becomes clear that there is not, anywhere in the world, any positive indicator pointing to the recovery of the economy!

We will mention below some of the data that indicate the continuation of the crisis:

1- The state of the economy in America:

The unemployment rate there has reached 8.9%, which is the highest rate in 26 years, and the level of national income fell by 6.1% in the first quarter of this year. In order for the volume of sales to match the goods, companies reduced the goods on offer to their lowest level since the Second World War, as they were reduced by the equivalent of 103.7 billion dollars in the first quarter of 2009, after being reduced in the fourth quarter of 2008 by 25.8 billion dollars. The volume of annual investments was reduced by 38%, and the volume of exports of goods and services fell by 30% in the first quarter of 2009, after falling by 23.6% in the fourth quarter of 2008. The number of foreclosures on mortgages because of inability to pay also rose in March 2009 to reach 341,180. This figure constitutes an increase of 17% since February 2009 and 46% since March 2008. Added to all of this is that the American government spent billions of dollars on the collapsed banks and on the lending companies. If this is the state of the United States, then no doubt the rest of the Western states suffer likewise.

2- The state of the economy in Germany:

The unemployment rate in Germany has reached 8.2%, and this is considered the worst recession since the Second World War. Were it not for the nearness of the elections and the government's way of announcing the unemployment rate, the announced unemployment rate would have been larger than this rate. The Federal Labour Office stated on 28/5/2009 that the rate of employees losing their jobs is increasing and that the real statistics of the rate of employees losing their jobs have been changed, this besides the reduction of daily working hours in an attempt to lessen the increase in the unemployment rate. The economic expert in the credit sector “Andreas Rees” noted that the unemployment statistics were manipulated to appear contrary to their reality, and to appear as though they improved in the month of June, as he said: “There is no doubt that there are numerous employees who will lose their jobs soon... the employment sector has remained the weak point on the road of the German economy's recovery.”

Furthermore, the managements of heavy factories and equipment factories expressed their concern that German industry is still weak globally and does not match global requirements.

The German engineering sector witnessed a decline at a rate of 58% in the month of April compared with last year, which is considered the biggest setback for this sector since its establishment, as the heavy factories' association said that “there has been a contraction in global demand to 60% and in domestic demand to 52%.” The German government, owner of the largest European economy, expects that it will contract by only 6% for this year, which is the lowest rate it has reached, and some economic observers are more pessimistic than the government.

3- The state of the economy in Europe in general:

Retail sales declined rapidly in the month of May 2009 because of the rise in the unemployment rate, that is, consumers refrained from spending, as the managers of “Bloomberg” companies saw that consumers are still hearing bad news about the labour market, that the unemployment rate will continue rising. Nick Kounis, head of European economists at Fortis Bank Nederland in Amsterdam, said: “Unemployment in Europe rose to 8.9% in March, which is the highest rate in three years, and the rate will rise next year to 9.9% and then to 11.5% in 2010, according to the European Commission.” And the economy of the Eurozone will contract by 4% this year according to the European Commission, because of the setback in exports and companies reducing the number of their workers.

4- The state of the economy in Japan:

The unemployment rate in Japan in the month of April 2009 reached 5%, which is the highest rate in five years. It was stated in the monthly report issued by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications that there are 3.46 million unemployed, which is 25.8% higher than the month of April last year. And there are only 46 jobs available for every 100 job seekers, which makes this rate the worst since 1999.

The government issued an index of the prices of main consumer goods, which showed a decline of 0.1% in the month of April compared with the same month of last year. The price index for consumer goods, which excludes the prices of fresh food, showed a decline in the month of March, which is its first decline in a year and a half, and it showed a decline in demand amid the global economic recession.

The rate of family spending in April also fell by 1.3% compared with the same month of last year, and family spending is considered a main indicator of private consumption, which accounts for more than half of Japan's gross domestic product. Japan's gross domestic product contracted by 10%, as the contraction of Japan's gross domestic product from the month of January to the month of March took a form that constituted the worst setback for the Japanese economy since 1947. “Glenn Maguire”, head of an Asian economics group, said: “In general a 10% decline in growth is considered a depression, and Japan almost reached this limit with the contraction of the Japanese economy by 9.7% during the current year. This confirms that the economic crisis has struck the Japanese economy, which is a developing economy, a severe blow.”

5- The state of the world economy:

Perhaps the most telling of indicators as to whether the world economy is on its way to recovery or not is the health of the current world economy. According to The New York Times newspaper, the economy in the developing states has gone through its worst quarter-year in decades. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said on 25/5/2009 that there are indicators that the worst is coming, and that the total gross domestic product of the thirty countries in the organisation contracted by 2.1% in the first quarter of this year compared with the quarter preceding it, and that if the rate settles at this figure, this decline will be the lowest since 1960, since the organisation began collecting such information. The national product of the organisation's members fell by 2% in the last quarter of 2008.

The economy of the states of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development constitutes 71% of the total world national income according to the World Bank. These economies contracted by 4.2% in the first quarter of last year. America's contribution to it was 0.9%, while Japan's share was 1%, the share of the 13 largest states in the Eurozone 1.3%, while the share of the remaining states was 1%. Whereas China, which is considered one of the few states not participating in the membership of the organisation, its economy continued to grow in the first quarter.

All of this indicates that the real reality of the world economy has not recovered from the economic crisis; rather, it is still suffering from it.

As for why the rise in the stock markets and in the prices of goods and services was noticed, it goes back to three reasons:

First: the American government's support of the insurance company (AIG) with 173 billion dollars of taxpayers' money, of which the company spent 90 billion dollars to pay its debts to American and European banks. On 15/3/2009 it became clear that the company (AIG) had distributed the money to numerous banks and institutions: the bank (Goldman) obtained a total of 12.9 billion dollars, the bank (Merrill Lynch) 6.8 billion dollars, the bank (Bank of America) obtained 5.2 billion, (Citigroup) obtained 2.3 billion dollars, (Wachovia) obtained 1.5 billion dollars, (Barclays) obtained 8.5 billion dollars, and the Swiss (UBS) obtained 5 billion dollars.

Regarding the importance of rescuing (AIG), the head of the American Federal Reserve (Ben S. Bernanke) commented by saying: “This company AIG made various unreasonable bets, and when the failure of those bets became clear, that company failed and the collapse occurred in the system of the financial markets.” And so that the government would not support those banks directly, for fear that this would lead to popular anger, the government supported the company AIG, which in its turn passed that money on to the banks. Consequently, numerous of those banks announced profits, such as (Bank of America), which announced profits of 4.2 billion dollars, (Citigroup) announced profits of 1.6 billion dollars, and (Goldman Sachs) 1.8 billion dollars. In Europe the bank (Barclays Bank) announced profits of 5.28 billion pounds sterling, so the shares of those banks rose.

In truth, this rise in share prices is not because of economic activity that caused a profit, but because of that support, whose effect will soon end.

Second: at the beginning of the current year the American government announced its programme to support the American banks, aimed at spreading a spirit of confidence among investors in the American banks, to suggest that they are well and not in great distress. The programme had been drawn up by the Secretary of the American Treasury (Timothy Geithner) to give the impression that most of the troubled bank assets could be written off the balance sheet. On the sixth of May 2009 the government announced that some banks, such as the bank (JP Morgan) and the bank (Goldman), are not in need of government support, while banks such as (Bank of America), (Morgan) and (Stanley) are in need of some support from the government. In the end result, the ten largest American banks need only 75 billion dollars, that is, this can be covered with complete ease and the government does not need to ask Congress for more support! This atmosphere and these statements caused the shares of the American banks to rise: the value of the shares of (Wells Fargo) rose by 8.5%, (Morgan Stanley) by 0.9%, (Bank of America) by 4% and (Citigroup) by 7%. It is clear that what happened is more like a propaganda, moral support to raise the shares, as speculators do by spreading certain news about the progress of a company's economic situation, or an expected progress for that company, so this leads to increased confidence and a rise in the share price; then after the purpose of the speculation has ended, the decline or collapse returns, as happened in the causes of the current economic crisis. Therefore, regardless of the state of joy that came over the investors, numerous observers said that the tests point to tragic results. For example, Mick Holland commented saying: “Carrying out tests of the markets is a waste of time.” And Yra Harris, a currency trader with the company (Praxis Trading), said: “At worst there is deception and a test of the wrong thing. For me, the mention of the unemployment rate, or that the group (Citigroup) is stronger than (JP Morgan), for me these are laughable matters, so I will be happy when these procedures end, and I will agree with the others who say that the structure of the banks has deteriorated in the past few years, and this is what explains their falling into chaos now.” On the fourth of May 2009 the global financial monitor estimated that the losses of the American financial institutions were 2.7 trillion dollars in the global credit crisis, that is, double the estimates that were issued six months earlier.

Third: at the beginning of this year both the American Federal Reserve and the British bank announced plans to begin buying the banks' bad assets, company bonds and other troubled financial assets. It is natural that increasing the pumping of money inevitably leads to inflation and a rise in the prices of goods and services, because increasing the money supply will lead to a weakening of purchasing power, and consequently inflation, that is, a rise in prices. The British bank has already begun expressing its concern at the rise in the rate of inflation in the economy, which led to the suffering of the economy as it reached its lowest level since 1930. A statement issued by the British bank said that “there are promising signs”, as the wheel of deterioration began to slow down. But the British bank also said that the slowdown is receding because of the rise in the rate of inflation, which has reached 2.9%, higher than the rate that had been expected, which is 2%. This is what explains the rise in the price of oil from 36 dollars to 58 dollars a barrel; that is, the rise in oil prices does not indicate an increase in demand for it, for energy consumption fell in 2009 for the first time since the Second World War, which clearly indicates that the world economy is very far from recovery. It is worth noting that oil prices usually increase when the value of the dollar is low; therefore the rise in the price of oil is not necessarily an indicator of an increase in demand for oil, because America monopolises the price of oil in order to prevent the collapse of the value of the dollar.

Accordingly, talk of the recovery of the Western economy is premature, and the Western governments' following of the policy of lowering the interest rate and buying bad assets is nothing but merely to postpone the economic collapse. Indeed, what is expected is that the Western governments' flooding of the markets with money will lead to inflation and the collapse of the commodities market, and the emergence of monetary bubbles, and then to a tragedy greater than what the world is witnessing now.
